title: Concerning the Secretaries of Princes
coreMove: Read and manage ministers as both proof of the prince's judgment and instruments whose interests must be bound to the state.
sourcePressure: The chapter says a prince is first judged by the people around him. Capable and faithful servants signal wise discrimination; bad servants reveal the prince's first error. The central test is whether the servant thinks first of the prince's affairs or of his own profit, and the prince keeps him honest by honor, riches, shared cares, and making clear he cannot stand alone.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The wrong version becomes hiring advice or team culture. The writer must show minister choice as a statecraft test: recognizing capacity, keeping fidelity, detecting self-profit, and binding the minister so honor and anxiety both attach him to the prince.

hook: hire smart people and trust them
counterintuition: most people assume leaders are judged by themselves, but actually by their team
good advisers make a weak prince wise
tryThisNow: set a timer for ninety seconds and list your team

exampleSpecs.domain: a treasury secretary handling war arrears while quietly buying claims through his cousins
exampleSpecs.audience: a prince testing whether a capable servant thinks first of private profit
exampleSpecs.stakes: the secretary can read every arrear account, but if he profits from the delay he holds the state for himself
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The prince places the cousin purchase slips under the arrears ledger and watches the secretary explain the state's need before he mentions his family's gain.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Cousin purchase slips peek from beneath a war arrears ledger.

exampleSpecs.domain: a map secretary whose border reports keep making the prince look wiser than his generals expect
exampleSpecs.audience: observers judging the prince through the quality of a technical servant he chose
exampleSpecs.stakes: if the prince can recognize the mapmaker's good and bad counsel, the servant cannot deceive him with specialized knowledge
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: After the map secretary marks two false passes, the prince corrects one and praises the other, proving he can judge what he cannot draft himself.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Two false-pass pins sit on a waxed border relief map.

exampleSpecs.domain: a royal seal keeper deciding whether to delay petitions until bribes arrive
exampleSpecs.audience: a ruler designing rewards and constraints that make fidelity more profitable than delay
exampleSpecs.stakes: the seal keeper touches every judgment, so private tolls at his desk become private rule over the state
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The ruler lays the honor chain, stipend roll, and public audit tablet beside the seal press, making the keeper rich, watched, and unable to stand alone.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A seal press sits between an honor chain and a public audit tablet.

exampleSpecs.domain: a naval stores minister who always proposes repairs that enrich his private dockyard
exampleSpecs.audience: a prince learning the never-failing self-interest test
exampleSpecs.stakes: the fleet may rot while the minister confuses his dockyard profit with the prince's need
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The prince asks for three repair options; the minister turns each hull token toward the same private dockyard mark before naming any naval danger.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Hull tokens point toward a private dockyard mark on a repair board.

exampleSpecs.domain: a chancery translator controlling foreign letters during a succession crisis
exampleSpecs.audience: a prince who cannot personally read every language but must not be ruled by the translator
exampleSpecs.stakes: one altered phrase can move allies, enemies, and marriage terms while appearing to be neutral service
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The prince compares the translator's smooth copy with a rough merchant gloss and asks why his own danger disappeared from the polished line.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A rough merchant gloss lies beside a polished chancery translation.

exampleSpecs.domain: a grain-port intendant whose honors are high enough to satisfy him but cares are heavy enough to keep him cautious
exampleSpecs.audience: a ruler building mutual trust with a strong servant instead of merely flattering him
exampleSpecs.stakes: too little honor breeds resentment, too much independent wealth breeds appetite, and no shared care lets him gamble with the prince's state
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The prince adds the intendant's name to the honor tablet, then hands him the winter shortage key so his prestige rises with the burden he must fear losing.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A winter shortage key rests below an honor tablet.

skillTargets: infer a prince's judgment from the quality and conduct of his ministers
apply the self-interest test to a servant who controls another's state
distinguish a wise prince who can judge advice from one ruled by a prudent servant
evaluate whether honors, riches, kindnesses, and shared cares bind a minister or enlarge his appetite

tryThisNowSpec: Pick one powerful adviser in a historical court or administration. Write what state matter they control, what private profit could distort them, and what honor or shared burden binds them to the ruler.
